deep.reconstruction:
The page has no formulas, only three pencil sketches. The reading below is interpretive and is marked as mine throughout.

(1) Top figure. There are two (possibly three) overlapping circles, each with a dot near its centre. This is the standard picture of analytic continuation: a function is given by a power series in one disc, and that disc overlaps a second disc centred at a point inside the first. On the overlap the second series is defined, so the function is carried into the second disc. (My interpretation: these are circles of convergence reaching toward singular points.)

(2) Middle figure. A horizontal line (the real axis) carries marks 0, 1, 2, with ∞ written beyond the right end. A closed oval runs around the segment from 0 to 1, and a fainter circle overlaps it. On my reading the singular points of a many-valued function lie at 0, 1, 2 and ∞. The oval is a closed path encircling the two branch points 0 and 1.

(3) Bottom figure. The same axis appears with 0, 1, 2 and ∞ (∞ drawn as a small loop at the right end of the line). Several overlapping ovals cover 0, 1 and 2. The segment 0–1 is drawn heavily, and a doubled line runs from 2 to ∞. The doubled line is the usual way of marking the two banks of a cut.

Together, (2) and (3) fit exactly the canonical two-sheeted Riemann surface of an elliptic irrationality, for example w^2 = z(z-1)(z-2), with branch points 0, 1, 2, ∞ and cuts along [0,1] and [2,∞).
- On such a surface, a loop around both 0 and 1 (figure 2) returns w to its original value, because the sign changes twice.
- That loop is one of the period cycles of ∫dz/w.
- Chains of overlapping discs (figures 1 and 3) are the means of continuing the function across the plane and seeing how the sheets join.

The context supports this. The previous page has sums of Abelian integrals, u_1 = ∫φ(z_1,s_1)dz_1 + ..., and curves with points s_0, s_1, z_0, z_1. The next page is a reading list (1853–55) that includes Hermite on the composition of Abelian functions. So this is most likely preparatory sketching for the theory of Abelian functions, published in 1857.

The following is my addition, not on the page. For the surface w^2 = z(z-1)(z-2):
- there are 2 sheets and 4 simple branch points;
- Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus g = 4/2 - 2 + 1 = 1;
- the real half-period is ∫_0^1 dx/√(x(1-x)(2-x)) = √2·K(1/2), in parameter notation.
errors: No derivations are written, so nothing can be wrong. The labels 0, 1, 2, ∞ and the drawing of the cuts are consistent with the standard two-sheeted elliptic surface.
The identification of the specific function, w^2 = z(z-1)(z-2), is conjectural.

results.what: Continuation of a function by a chain of overlapping discs of convergence (top and bottom figures)
results.modern_name: Analytic continuation along chains of discs
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (systematised in the 1840s–1870s); Cauchy and Riemann used it implicitly

results.what: Real axis with branch points 0, 1, 2, ∞; cut along [0,1] and a double-banked cut from 2 to ∞; closed loop enclosing the branch points 0 and 1
results.modern_name: Two-sheeted Riemann surface of an elliptic (genus-1) curve with branch cuts; a period cycle encircling a cut

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only rough sketches of disc continuation and branch cuts on the real axis. These are standard elements of Riemann's own published theory of Riemann surfaces and Abelian functions, and nothing goes beyond his known work.

checkable.asserts: Riemann–Hurwitz: a 2-sheeted cover of the sphere with 4 simple branch points (0, 1, 2, ∞) has genus 1.
The integral across the cut [0,1] equals sqrt(2)*K(m=1/2), so this difference is approximately 0 (an interpretive check on the conjectured curve).
Encircling two square-root branch points (0 and 1) changes the sign of w twice, so w returns to itself (the difference is 0).

transcription_corrections: Top figure: there are two large overlapping circles plus a smaller overlapping oval on the left, with roughly three dots, not just two circles.
Middle figure: '∞' is written separately, well beyond the right end of the line. A faint second circle overlaps the oval around 0–1.
Bottom figure: the right end of the doubled line ends in a small loop, which is likely the '∞' label. The segment 0–1 is drawn heavily, with ticks at 0 and 1.
